s01.text: In 2020 NVIDIA noticed something. Deep learning did not need FP32's precision, but it did need FP32's range.

s02.text: So they made a new sixteen-bit format that keeps the range and throws away the precision.

s03.text: FP16 has five exponent bits and ten mantissa bits. BF16 has eight and seven.

s04.text: Same sixteen bits. A completely different number.

s05.text: The range is what a training run needs. Gradients get tiny. Activations get huge. Neither is a problem if the exponent can reach.

s06.text: The precision is what inference likes. A weight at BF16 has fewer significant digits than one at FP16.

s07.text: Which is why BF16 is the training format and FP16 is still the inference format.

s08.text: And why both are everywhere: BF16 where the range matters, FP16 where the precision does.

s09.text: The interesting part is what the throwaway bits buy. BF16 keeps the exponent identical to FP32.

s10.text: Which means a BF16 number and an FP32 number have exactly the same exponent range.

s11.text: You can convert between them by shifting bits. No rounding, no range check.

s12.text: FP16 needs a clamp, because its exponent cannot represent FP32's biggest and smallest values.

s13.text: The most useful number format is the one that is boring to convert.
